blocks.x: He's 87 years old. I was thinking he was a little bit older.
Huh? I thought he was a little older.
He could be older than that, I don't know. I wonder where his birth certificate is.
He could be in the church. He had to get to the church, the St. Augustine church.
We could check that easy, Bill. Yeah. You were talking about, who was that, an uncle of yours or somebody, a clarinet player?

My uncle, Louis Arthur Dahl, yeah, they say that he was one of the best, I mean, in those times, in those days, you know. That's when my father first started playing, you know. And I might have always told me that, I would just say that before he died he wrote some nice music. He wrote a beautiful waltz, beautiful waltz, beautiful pox style, but they never could find the music of music. I mean, someone took it. Got misplaced, something like that. It was beautiful.
Well, at one time, your father said that he was the only good clarinet player? In those days, yeah, in those days.

But later on in years, I mean, around about 1910, when I remember my father of the bands, I knew who was the best clarinet player at that time. Because they had George Bakke and Lores Atillo. Well, they had other clarinet players, but they didn't come up to those guys. I think George was the best. Because any time they played a funeral, I remember they played a funeral on, they had a funeral on St. Anthony, between St. Claude and Lores. And she was a saloon called Delio. These people have a shoe store right here on the hop in Claiborne, I can't think of their name. Well, it was right next door, at that time, those people were living there, had a little shoe place there. This was starting to sell shoes, you see? Heckman or something like that? Heckman, that's right, Heckman. Those Heckman people, that's right. And it was about two years away from then, this person, this fellow had died. And George was knowing, George Bakke was knowing to make, any time they played a funeral, and he picked up the clarinet. I mean, everybody had tears in their eyes in those days. That's right, George Bakke, he's a fine looking man. I used to think that he was a pretty man. I was small, you know, I thought he was pretty looking. He had a face like a girl, like a woman. But he could play. Oh, he could play. Gee whiz. I never heard nothing like him, no more after that.
On the street they played E flat?

E flat, yeah, he played the E flats. Now, Larenza Tio, I mean, young Larenza, I mean, he was a very good clarinetist. Charlie McCurtis, he was good. They had Alphonse P. Kool, and I'm talking about the guys that could read at that time. I can remember, they had, you know, Big Al Lover, he was around that time, but he was a musician with those guys. He played Ratty, you know, he was a ratty kind of player. Later on in the years, well, I mean, what, Basher and them fellas came up with. But that Basher, Sidney Basher, he was the most.
Well, who took his place after he left? Who's that? Basher has been the tops.
Has been the tops.
Or writing music.
Well, I remember at, at Villery and then they had a boy they called Williams, I can't think of his other name. He died in California. He and Basher tied up and it was, it was about even, even.
You'd say Basher was right at the top though, would you?

He was top, yeah. He was, he was wonderful. And that Basher could take, I remember that, Buddy Petit and them on top. They hired him to play the advertising. And at that time Bob Lyons was working in the pawn shop on Ramport and Pedita. Bob Lyons, the bass player. And Basher didn't have no clarinet. I remember this, I recall that good girl, I used to follow all the bands. So they said we're going to get him a clarinet. The wagon pulls up with the horse in it, up at a pawn shop and they told, told Bob Lyons that Basher didn't have no clarinet. And went and got an old clarinet, looked like, it was like a banana sort of. I mean the color of a banana.
Yeah, the brown one. I've seen it.

Yeah, the color of a banana, because it was kind of yellow. And man, I didn't know how long that clarinet had been in that pawn shop. And Basher fixed the reed on there and I know some of the notes didn't blow. Man, that man could play. Wow, what came out that clarinet. And the notes that didn't work, he didn't mind that. He didn't mind that all along. That man was great. Did you ever hear him on trumpet? How's that?
Did you ever hear Sidney play trumpet?
Yeah, I heard him play a parade on trumpet on Seminart Street. During the day they had all the rocks, the big rocks on them.
Cobblestones.

In the street area, cobblestones. I mean, they were short of a, well they had, I think they had about three or four bands in that parade. But they were short of a trumpet player. So, I guess Basher didn't play trumpet, I guess. He got a trumpet and played. He played all the parade. I remember that one good.
On Seminart Street.
Right at that time he was living on the, Maree between Ennet and Saint-Etna. Yeah, that guy was great.

I wanted to ask a little bit before we got about your family background. Being a French name, you told me once somebody had checked the name way back to France. Do you know anything about your father's name?

Yeah, well no. You know, some people was trying to tell me when I was working at the Jazz Limited, that they have a lot of barbers in a little town near Paris. And he said that he's going to, I don't know how he's going to find that out. He's going to look up and see if they're relative to me. You don't think about your father's folks?
How is that? You don't think about your father's folks?
No, I don't know anything. I don't know if my sister may even tell you because you heard my mother and my grandmother talk about that sometimes.
They came from France though I suppose.

Well, his father, he's great grandfather, his grandfather at least, not his father. His grandfather I think was white. He's a little bit. Yeah. Yeah. That's, well you know people in those days, you know what I mean. I sure am. People migrated from France, you know, mixed with colored women, you know how that was. So that's, that's how most, all the people had. French names I imagine, or Spanish names, I mean that's, colored people, you know what I mean. How that?
It was legal in those days.
Well yeah, I imagine it was legal, yeah. No law against marriages, is it?
How is that? There was no law against marriages. No, there was no law.
There was no law in those days, that's what I understand, there was no laws in those days.
I wanted to ask you how you got your first name, were your name left anybody?
No, no, no, this nickname, I tell you all, my first cousin, and his sister, and my sister, this sister here, you mean my nickname T-Bar?
No, no, Paul, your name left. Oh, Paul, well that's my middle name.
My first name was, I don't like to call it, I don't like that name. I don't like to call myself that name.
Well you won't tell anybody it's Alvin.
My name, I'll tell it to you, my name is Adolph Paul Barbera, Adolph. Adolph Paul Barbera. And you were? I speak about my nickname, how I got the nickname.
I thought maybe you were named after Shalini or somebody, I don't know.
Shalini, well yeah, that's how I got my name. From him? From Paul, yeah, Paul Shalini, my godfather.
Somebody had told me that.
You forgot to ask my father about Paul Shalini. Yeah, you forgot to ask him, but I couldn't think, you know. If I had told him I'd have marked some of the things down, you know, to ask him, you know.
Were they close friends, your father and father?
Yeah, were they close friends, yeah. They were neighbors, you know. They were next door to each other. They were neighbors.
How did, and what did he play Paul Shalini?

Well I don't know what he played. I know the clarinet was, one of his instruments, but he taught all the instruments. He taught everything. Because that's when I, before he started taking a clarinet, I went to him, you know. And he was going to teach me. But I decided I want the low end drums. I heard Red Happy and Henry Zeno and all, Mac Morris and all those guys. And I said, well, I'll switch the drums. So there you are. But clarinet, I really don't want a clarinet. I was cut out for clarinet. I don't know why. I didn't take it out. I'm sorry too. You know where I'm real sorry. That's right. Because you know, I have good ideas. I know how it goes. I know the turns, you know. I know just how it's supposed to be played.
How did you get the name of T-Boy too?

How did you get the name of T-Boy? Well, I tell you, my cousin, first cousin was named Mac Boy. And his sister, they named his sister, Mac T-Girl. So, they named my sister, this one here, T-Girl. Then they named me T-Boy. That was nicknames, you know. T-Boy, T-Girl, Mac Boy, Mac T-Girl. That's how I got the name.
Does it mean anything? How? Does it mean anything? Is it tea? Is it tea you drink?

Well, I imagine it was tea you drink. I don't know. I don't know. Why they call us that? I don't know anything. That's what I mean. That's what I mean. Maybe because it's small. Yeah, maybe from the French, huh?
Petit. Yeah, petite.
Yeah, little children, you know. Petit, yeah, that's right. That's probably it.
That's right, probably it, yeah.
Probably it. We didn't get your birth date on this.
We interviewed you for life and we have a copy of that. Yeah, you have a copy of that for life.

You might get this for a copy of that. I don't know you interviewed me. Well, you know how I would say, I'm going to, I'm going to, I'm going to, I'm going to tell no Stuart on this. No, we won't tell the same thing.
I just thought that we, you were born in 1900, was it? 19-1.

19-1. Oh, I wasn't born in 19-1. I was born another day, but I ain't going to tell you another day. 19-1, let's let it go to 19-1. Your sister's younger than you are. Oh, yeah, she's much younger than you.
You have a good memory to remember all those things your father told you.

Yeah, well you see, we wasn't kids that would run the street, we'd be in the house and they'd tell us all things. No, we'd be in the house. And they'd tell us all things, you see. And with him talking and we'd listen to him because we'd always be in the house.

I was telling a time that, I remember a time when it Van Dylons, I think you remember that, on St. Anthony between, two of those from Heckman. Heckman, selling shoes, selling shoes, I mean, you know, that's been a long time.
Oh, yeah, that's a long time.

That's been a long time. I was telling about George Barquet, you know, how great he was, people used to cry, he used to make tears, that's on the clarinet player. I've seen that made the people cry, talking about clarinet players today, shame on them.
They don't have no musicians. No, shame on them.

You should hear those bands in those days, like the Olympia band, Superior band, and Imperial band, those was bands. And the parade, does he like the Armand Brass band? I mean, well, the Armand Brass band, I mean, they played my father, I mean, he can't tell you about that, because you didn't ask him about that. But I can tell you, they played ball house music. You can forget about what he said about the other fellas, you know, reading at that time. Yeah, but later on in the years, I mean, it was a Ball House band. Well, like you said, Danny Lewis on bass drum, well, they used them sometimes. But the main drummer that I seen played bass drum with the Armand Brass band was Bebe, or the, Jean-Vin and Bebe Matthews. He was two good drummers. And they played bass drum. No, he used to play a snare drum, but they, Bebe Matthews played. And Bill, Bill Matthews was a good drummer too, don't forget that. He was one of the top drummers you had too. He was in that category too. Well, they had, in that band, the Armand band, Bebe Matthews, Jean-Vin, they had Buddy Johnson on trombone. They had Vic Gasper on baritone, my daddy on alto. They had Manny Perez, Joe Oliver, and Kimball. Sometime they'd have Pete, Pete Bocas. But those three was the great guys. And did they play? Manuel Perez, Joe Oliver, and Kimball.
Who were the Ball House men in that band?

Who was the Ball House men in that band? Joe Oliver. He was the man. Joe Oliver, you know, he played, you know, like you have a third trumpet player on the end in the orchestra. Well, that's where Joe was in that band. But Manuel, I mean, he was just a, he made tunes, but you know, good tunes, but not like Joe. Joe was always, I mean, Joe was always like, you know, Ball House, like Lil Armstrong or Buddy Boll or something like that. You know, people like that.
He never used a mute in the orchestra. Who was that?
No, he never used, no, no mute.
They put their hands in front of the horns then? No, no, not in the street, no, no.

They just played, they played though. When you heard those bands coming down the street talking about Eureka, and these little bands, little bands you hear today, I'm not panning them to be good these days. But, I mean, you couldn't do no comparison. Oh no, man, no comparison. No comparison, man. You all don't hear the real thing. It's too bad. Couldn't catch those people on tape. No. Catch them trumpet players, liking people. Butter Petit. Walter Blue, huh?
Walter Blue, oh. He was a good trumpet player.
He died on the street. Yeah, he died on the street. He died playing the parade.
Yeah, he fell asleep. Who ought to talk to his son?
Walter Blue, he was good. His son played something.
Huh? His son plays millionaires. Oh yeah. He might remember something, Bill. Yeah. He was too small, but his mother could tell.
I had a man of trumpet players in those days. I mean, they had Chip, they had Joe Johnson, they had, let's see, come on trumpet players. Edwin Clemons, he was good. So many guys.
Who was Chip?

Chip, he was a trumpet player, but now he plays, I think he threw around the base now. He racks ball up on Rampart and he ran, I think it is. He ran, yeah. Oh yeah. Yeah. Should have shot by. He was a good man.
Is that Dave Brown's ball, you know?
I don't know his ball. No, that ain't Dave Brown's ball. No, no. That's coming down. Coming down. And not on that side of the street.
From the Lakeside. Yeah.
Lakeside, that's right.
He used to play shows with Johnny Marl. That's right, yeah.

He played with him. We had a many good musicians, good drummers. Many good drummers. Mack Murray, Walter Brundy. Walter Brundy, Walter Brundy, Leon, he played clarinet. He was pretty fair. They had, they had, they had, Tick Chambers, he was a pretty good trumpet player too, Tick Chambers. Never hear a fella named Ned. Ned, yeah.
Was that his last name or first name? No, I don't remember.
Ned. Who did he play with?
Seen different bands, you know.

But those bands, I mean Imperial and I just can't, I just can't recall these people, they're playing music, but these fellas, I mean, oh man, they played. You see the Scott Joplin books, all those rags, you don't hear none of that music. And them guys just took that music and played that music and didn't have the jazz, just play it. Just play it, man. So beautiful, man. All those, Maple Leaf Rag, Grayson Buta, African Pass, Ophelia Rag, Entertainer's Rag. Oh man, oh, I used to play all those tunes, you know. Of course at that time I didn't read, you know, tell them, I was guessing, you know. I was a pretty good guesser. Yeah, I was a pretty good guesser. Yeah.
Did you ever hear of Chris Kelly's one?
I work at Chris Kelly.
He was a Bell House musician.
Was he a Bell House musician? Chris Kelly, he stopped on the street there and he'd take that glass, take that glass,
and I'm glad I'm muting. That's a point on the story.
That's a point on the story. That's a point on the story. That's a point on the story. I recall one time I played a pick-need with him.
I'ma lead it out.

You're gonna leave out about that? I'ma lead it out on the lake there. I'll tell you about what they did to him. I don't know. I was playing a pick-need with Basia and Buddy Petit out there, out the lake, I forget who I was in that band. And some guys from Irish Channel had hired us. And while we was on the mission, the guy took all our coats and tied them all in and not, man. And put them back on the chair where we had over there. Tied them all in and not, boy. Got this some... Did you work in the channel?
Huh? You ever work in the channel much?

Yeah, I played a lot of dance with... Well, later on in the year I played in the channel a lot with Kid Punch and Bang. Yeah, Kid Punch and Bang. Yeah, Kid Punch and Bang. Quiet, quiet? Was it quiet? No, no, them Irish's, man. They're tough, man. Them people. Oh, them is tough. In those days, those people is tough, man. They start a fight, man. Woo, woo. Never knew when that fight was gonna end, man. Gee, where is it?
What did you do when the fight stopped? When the fight stopped?

Just get out the way, move out the way. Try and protect my drums and get out the way. Well, they never bothered us. I mean, they'd be fighting amongst themselves. But they was good people, though. They were really nice. I played a lot of jobs up there with Kid Punch's band, Irish Channel. Kid Punch had so much work. At that time, I had to carry my drums, you know, from down here and all the way up to the Irish Channel. You see, you wouldn't lie on a street car. Or you'd catch a ride, somebody, you know, with a wagon or float was going up and I asked them, you know, give you a lift, you see. And sometime when we played, Irish Channel, I'd have to leave. The job was for 8 o'clock. Well, I'd put my drums on my back at 5 o'clock in the evening to get there for 8. I'd walk way up in Carlton, way up in Carlton, way up in St. Charles. You know, protection and everything, you have jobs like that. And I had a bass player, whoever the bass player was, I mean, at that time, we'd walk together. We'd meet one another. Who was the bass player? Gabe. A fella called Gabriel. We called him Gabe. I think he's still around. He was a Bob, I don't know. Tell me he's still around, I haven't seen him. And he was a hard workin', hard workin' bass player. Work hard all the time, Gabe. That's a good band we had. Ada Morris and the band Trombone, Punch. I don't know, Georgia Boyd. I can't think, Preston. Preston played the band, that's right. And Gabe played the bass. They had so many jobs, until I quit the band. I got a job going at Tom Anderson in 1922. Yeah, it was 22, I think it was 22. And I quit the band. I had too much work. I said, Ty Kennedy's just punch. And I think, I think it was Leroy replacement. I think it was Leroy Evans.
When did Chani play with Punch? Before you or after?

Oh, I don't remember. At that time Punch, Chani was playin' with Papa Salisbury. At that time, yeah. He must have played after, maybe afterwards. That's a guy who had a big reputation. Don't know how he could go back at it. He played good drums. What Chani would be? Oh, he was a good drummer.
He was a good drummer.
He was a good drummer. I don't understand it. He's sick.
Huh? He's sick. He's sick now.
Yeah, he's sick now. He came up with us.
He was raised in the same neighborhood.
Yeah, raised in the neighborhood. Yeah.
Did he start out about the same time as you?

No, I think after me, you know. He came after me. After me. My first job was with, remember Johnny Pernodon? Yeah. When I was working at Sancho Hotel. That's right. And I saved that money. My mom told me to take that $25 and pay on a set of drums. Yeah. And the same day I got the drums, Johnny Pernodon needed a drummer. Uh-huh. And they came by the house in Harvard. That was my first job. We played for some campaign down on the Center Rock and Charter. By a bar. I mean, political thing, you know what I mean?
He used to break all the scenes out of my mother's chairs. Playing drums.
And that was my first job. To play professionally, you know. From then on, I went on up.
What year was that? You started with that? About 15, huh?
About 15. About 1915. And we lost my sister. My sister.

You know, I've been about 25. Huh? No, he wasn't that old. You weren't 25 years old. No. I didn't know much. I was a little. I had to put on long pants to go play. I had to put on long pants to go play. 16 or 15 years old when he started. I don't know if he was that. No. I had to put on long pants to go play. I had to put on long pants to go play. 16 or 15 years old when he started. I don't know if he was that. No. He was stabbed in heaven. He had to put on long pants. He had to put on long pants because he was in short pants.

And then when I used to go work in the red light district. I used to go over there, he'd come and get me a little little fellow, a little kind of trouble, a friend of my union. Come at the house and tell me his dad said to go to his place at Rice's. And I put on, I had a pair of old long pants and stripes and it was heavy, big summertime, heavy piece of goods. And I put those long trousers on and go up there and play. Play with Manion and them. Manion and Francis had to wake Rice. They'd wake there a long time, long time. And a couple of times I went with King Oliver, with Joe Oliver, I mean, I worked at Pete Lada's place. I worked at Henry Zeno's place. Put on long trousers. I worked at Fue Clothes, guys, who I was drumming there. I think this boy would die, play a snare drum with John Kazmi. What's his name, Roger? Roger. Roger, I used to go to these places at Fue Clothes. Who was his band at Fue Clothes?
I loved it a kid. Whose band was at Fue Clothes?
I don't know whose band was at Fue Clothes. He probably started when he was buried here. I know Roy Palmer was working there, I remember that. I remember that good who was working there.
Was Sidney Dazmine's there?
I think Sidney Dazmine was working there, if I can recall. It had been so long ago, I forgot.
Do you remember pianist Thomas, George W. Thomas? Do you remember ever?
Yeah, piano player? Yes. Yeah, big George. Big George Thomas, yeah, I know him, yeah.
He worked there, I think, for a while.

I think he was working there at that time, if I'm not mistaken. I think he was. I can't recall, I mean, who was working there. I remember Roy Palmer working there. That's a trombone player. Talk about getting the gutter trombone player. He was that, I don't know where he is now. But ain't nobody had no shame on Uri. That's right. Shame on Uri, Uri ain't no stuff for him. I'm gonna tell you what I feel about it, you know what I mean? Of course, you know, I hate to say those things, you know what I mean? Because guys want to be the greatest, you know what I mean? But if a man was coming to him, Roy Palmer could put you in the gutter.
How about Zoo? Do you remember Zoo Robinson? Zoo, yeah.
Yeah, I remember Zoo spitting all off that tailgate, yeah. Yeah, he played a many avatars, Zoo Robinson. He was a good, good, good man, good musician.
Johnny St. Cyr gave me an invitation. I mean, spitting everything, and every time he'd spit. Don't you remember Zoo Robinson playing the trombone? I think so.
Was he ratty at all? Huh? Was he ratty at all? Who ratty?
Did he play by ear? No, he was a good musician. I mean, he could play by ear too.
The thing you want to know is that ratty stuff, eh? He should have been bone in those days when they had, he should have been about this time when they had the ratty stuff.
Yeah, he could.
About the edgy, he was a ratty stuff.
You'd have a book about that big. Yeah, about that big stuff. Two feet high. About that high you'd have a book.
They don't have any more carnival, you know. The carnival we had was so much different than the carnival now. Oh, yeah.
No carnival.

The culture with masks and all, they had good bands and good parades and everything. They don't have no carnival. No, they don't have no carnival. People want to go out and worry about carnival mostly for kids. No carnival. They sang, they danced, they danced. They sang carnival, no.

I mean, those days it was carnival. They do their best on carnival. I mean, everybody, nobody, nobody, nobody went to the street with our mask. Nobody went to the street with our mask. And they didn't want to do under that mask.
Yeah, sure. They danced and play a joke on people, you know. That's right.
Women, you know, get out and boy, you ain't no good, you ain't no good, you ain't no good, you know, so-and-so-and-so. And they go about a business.

But who was that? Who was that? You know what I mean? Come to my room or something, give him a key. And he thought, sure, he was going to that garage room. And he wasn't going nowhere because he just had those keys delivering them around to all of us. They had fun. It was really fun, you know. And the fellas would dance, mask like a woman, dress up like a woman.
Yeah, dress up like a woman.
And they danced with the men and the men would buy him a whole lot of drink.

I mean, I danced with a guy one night at the Columet Hall and I thought he was a girl. Really? All night long. I didn't get angry, there was nothing to get angry about, you know. Some people, you know, in a fight, want to shoot you, you know. I mean, no, but, no, that wasn't.

That's what happened when my daddy got shot. He didn't want to say, but that's what happened. A fella was dressed up as a woman dancing with another fella. And when the fella, he was a woman, a man, he started to fight and that's when he shot him, when he was trying to get away from him.
That's what mom said.
Yeah. What would they sing? Huh? What would they sing? Sing all kinds of French songs, Creole songs and all. Oh yeah, Creole songs. Do you know any of them? Uh-uh.
Just a few words, I mean, he used to say most of them, he'd say, ay ay ay ay, mu pala meh sa, mu pala meh sa, mu pala meh sa.
What does that mean? I don't like that.
I don't like that. I don't like that.
I don't like that.

Yeah, they were good. You would sing all kinds of Creole songs, they'd put all kinds of words in them. Well, they know how to talk, that kind of stuff, you know. Yeah, they'd say, oh, they'd make a real song, they'd rhyme it after.
Yeah, it was good days.
Did your father speak Creole? No. French. My mother and my father. My whole family. My mother and my father.
My whole family. My mother and my father, my mother and my father, my mother and my mother, excuse me. Yeah, I'm going to speak good French.
We should speak, but we never did battle.
She hardly ever say anything in American. American.
She'd always talk French.
And she spoke to him all the time. She'd be in the kitchen, I mean, all the time. We understood it, but we never did.
We understood it.

We were going to pick it up and go fast, to ride fast like they did. But everything they said, they said in French. My grandmother, all of them. They'd be in the kitchen. They'd go, get it, get it, get it, get it, get it, get it. Well, we'd understand what they're saying, you know. But we couldn't answer fast like they couldn't answer, but we had to take our time and answer.
When your father went to school, was that a French school when he was a boy, you suppose? I guess it was.
I imagine it was. He thought I'm French, you know. Yes. You don't know how old. Most of those people were Frenchmen, you know.
You don't know if he had any music in the school or just studied with this man from the French opera? How long he studied? Did you ever hear him sing?
No, no, I never did say.
You see, he's not much of a talker, my daddy. You all got a lot out of him because my mother made conversation with us, but we didn't talk. No, he didn't talk much.
I see. No, he's always serious.
He didn't talk much. He talked to her and what we caught, we caught it from my mother.
But you all were looking at him.
But my mother, she's there. You all were lucky because he's not, he'd stay back there in that room all day and he would say two words to you. That's just his disposition.
That's his disposition. You all have been quiet.
He's on the quiet type.
He could out walk in a musician living. That man you see that can't walk right now.
And he didn't have no friends, you know what I mean?

All day long. Never sweat. Never pressed bottle. I don't care how hot the sun was. Any old musician could tell you. Maybe Harrison Boyle you're talking, him he'll tell you why. I walk, never get tired. Better fellas be tired and just walk. And those days, I mean they played parade from 8 in the morning to about 6 in the evening. Just walk.
They didn't have no streets like they have now.
No, no street lights that got nice.
And the same and all street over there. They had big stones like that. Big rocks, big stones like that. And they had big old trees that'd be over together.
And all the big stones. And Espinay Street all that was big stones. That's right, big stones. And those days when you're walking, you're walking like that. All Seminoles. And they walked on our lap.
We were little bit of kids.
All that was rock. I mean, all the street was rock. Big stones and all.
Stones and all.
